subject: ONNX cache warmup + throughput safety matrix for private GPU pool

From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>, Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>, Brightline Health <ops@brightline.health>
Cc: AWS Partner <aws-sales@amazon.com>
Date: Wed, 30 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: ONNX cache warmup + throughput safety matrix for private GPU pool

Team / Brightline ops —

Thanks for the call earlier. Per Brightline's ask, I sketched a proposal for how we should size the private GPU pool to meet their sustained and burst throughput while keeping tail latency within SLAs. High-level asks we should answer in this thread:

- Sustained throughput target: what we size for (QPS / tokens/sec) for steady state
- Burst absorption headroom: how many GPUs and warm containers needed to cover 3–5x sudden spikes
- ONNX / quantized model warmup pattern: warm vs. lazy load, prefetch sequence, and KV/embedding cache priming
- Network & egress considerations: sustained egress bandwidth and connection churn when cold-starts spin up
- Fallback and cost tradeoffs: cheaper quantized variants vs. cold fallback to hosted model

Attached: pool_provisioning_matrix.xlsx (matrix of scenarios), onnx_warmup_playbook.md (proposed warmup scripts and ordering), latency_sim_results.pdf (sim outputs from staging sims).

Initial assumptions I used in the matrix: Brightline steady-state 1.2k QPS (in their note), typical p95 target: 150 ms for single-turn generation at 1–2k tokens average, expected peak spikes to ~6k QPS lasting 5–10 minutes. Network egress per request estimated at ~120 KB for heavy responses (including embeddings).

Immediate asks:
1) Marissa — can you validate the warmup sequence and the estimated VM->GPU spin timing we used? I assumed 40–60s for VM attach + 15–25s for model warm / ONNX cache load.
2) Jonas — please sanity-check the safety matrix (attached) for GPU headroom and warm-pool sizing; flag any cost-levers we should present to Brightline (reserved nodes vs. burst on shared infra).
3) Brightline ops — confirm spike shape (duration and amplitude). If your peaks are longer than 10 minutes we need to rethink runway.

Goal: agree on a recommended provisioning matrix by end of week and a 1-week soak plan for staging.

Thanks,
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Platform Partnerships
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: ONNX cache warmup + throughput safety matrix for private GPU pool

Thanks Vanessa, quick read-through and a few notes:

- Warmup sequence: agree on prefilling ONNX runtime artifacts into GPU memory before model init. Proposed order in the playbook is good but swap the KV cache priming to earlier in the sequence (do KV priming immediately after kernel load). That reduces first-request p95 by ~20% in our sims.
- Timings: the 40–60s attach window is reasonable for cold attach in our current infra; for on-prem we can get that down to ~25–35s with warm-container snapshots. Add a "snapshot warm-pool" column in the matrix (I added a draft in the spreadsheet).
- Warm-pool sizing heuristic: keep warm pool at ~15% of sustained GPUS for multi-tenant oversubscription, but for Brightline given their sensitivity I'd recommend 25% reserved warm nodes for peak-critical routes.

I added two rows to pool_provisioning_matrix.xlsx: one for standard warm snapshot strategy and one for aggressive cold-to-warm prefetch (higher cost). Also added p95 estimates for each scenario.

Next step: If Brightline confirms spike length/shape, I'll update the matrix with revised p95 and cost delta.

- Marissa
Principal SRE, Serving Runtime

Copying in a couple of operational guardrails and a proposed provisioning matrix variant (see spreadsheet v2):

- Provisioning variant A (conservative reserved): reserve 100% of steady-state GPUS + 30% warm nodes for short spikes. Pros: predictable latency and simple billing, Cons: cost heavier for client.
- Provisioning variant B (elastic burst): reserved for 80% steady-state, autoscale up to 4x for bursts using warm snapshots on a shared burst pool. Pros: cost efficient, Cons: requires cross-customer QoS and stricter tenancy rules.

Fallback behavior: if ONNX cache load fails or kernel mismatch, route to a hosted fallback model with rate-limited traffic (configurable) while we warm the private nodes. Add a circuit-breaker at 1% error spike or p99 latency > 1s for >30s.

Operational ask for Brightline: we need a 48-hour maintenance window allowance to deploy warm-snapshot agents and a single blast test (5–10 minute controlled spike) during the onboarding week. We'll run a soak test in staging for 7 days at 75% sustained load + periodic 5-minute spikes to validate cache/prefill logic.

Cost note: I added a model in the sheet that shows incremental monthly cost for each variant; difference between A and B is roughly 18–30% depending on burst frequency. We'll highlight the tradeoffs in the handoff.

-Jonas
VP, Product Operations

Vanessa / team —

Thanks for the clear plan and the matrix. Quick clarifications from Brightline ops:

- Confirmed sustained target: 1,200 QPS (95% of traffic). Bursts: we see up to 5.5–6.5k QPS in product-driven events, typically 4–12 minutes in length. Rare longer spikes reported historically (1–2x per quarter) lasting up to ~25 minutes.
- SLA tolerance: p95 under 200 ms is acceptable for now; p99 must not exceed 1.2s for critical routes.
- Security/KMS: model keys are rotated weekly and must not be exported. Any warm-snapshot procedure must integrate with our KMS policies (we cannot store unwrapped model artifacts outside customer VPC).
- Maintenance window: 48 hours fine; prefer it on a weekend. We can do a controlled blast test during onboarding week — target June 11-17 (we can pick a day).

We appreciate the fallback hosted route suggestion. If you can provide the hosted fallback endpoint and expected degradation behavior, we can bake that into our incident playbook.

We'll review the spreadsheet and get back with confirmation of maintenance date & preferred contact for the blast (ops lead: Maria Chen <maria.chen@brightline.health>).

Regards,
Amit Patel
Platform Ops, Brightline Health
